source: Quinlan (1990) Learning logical definitions from relations (FOIL)
finding: FOIL learns function-free Horn clauses from relational tuples. It extends the greedy covering method of attribute-value learners (ID3 style) to first-order logic. Literals are chosen by an information-gain style heuristic, and a bit-encoding cost stops clauses that cost more than they explain.
numbers: Six tasks (family relations, list and graph relations, chess endgame, card game rule, etc.). Family trees: FOIL correct on 78 of 80 test cases over 20 trials, vs 7 of 8 for Hinton's neural net; 11 s per trial.
limits: Greedy, one clause at a time. Needs both positive and negative tuples. Small test set in the family task (4 per trial).
agent_relevance: Shows the basic recipe: build a rule literal by literal, score each step by how many examples it separates. A cheap counted score can drive rule building without model opinion.

source: Quinlan (1990) Learning logical definitions from relations (FOIL) - chess endgame
finding: On the King-Rook vs King illegal-position task, FOIL beat the earlier clause learners CIGOL and DUCE in accuracy and time, even though no exact definition exists in the given relations.
numbers: 100 training positions: CIGOL 77.2% (21.5 hr), DUCE 33.7% (2 hr), FOIL 92.5% sd 3.6 (1.5 s). 1000 training: DUCE 37.7% (10 hr), FOIL 99.4% sd 0.1 (20.8 s). Test: 5,000 unseen positions for the others, 10,000 for FOIL; FOIL averaged over 10 runs, the others 5.
limits: Cross-paper comparison on different machines. About 34% of positions are illegal.
agent_relevance: Imperfect but accurate rules are acceptable: rank rule candidates by held-out accuracy, not by exactness (links G3).

source: Quinlan (1990) FOIL - limitations section
finding: Author lists FOIL limits: function-free Horn clauses only, cannot postulate new predicates, needs negative tuples, not incremental, greedy and short-sighted, only discrete constants, no notion of proof.
numbers: Implementation capped at 128 constants, so lists up to length five could not be handled. append took 188 s, reverse 247 s (Shapiro 1981 reported 11 and 6 s for his system on different hardware).
limits: Self-reported in 1990; later systems fixed several (predicate invention, recursion).
agent_relevance: These limits (greedy search, no invented concepts, needs counter-examples) are the failure modes a prompt-based rule proposer also shows.

source: Cropper, Dumancic, Evans, Muggleton (2021/22) Inductive logic programming at 30
finding: ILP induces a logic program from examples plus background knowledge (BK). Unlike vector ML it learns relations. Claimed strengths: data efficiency (often one example), BK reuse, expressivity, explainability.
numbers: Old systems compared: FOIL, Progol, Aleph, TILDE, HYPER. New: ILASP, Metagol, dILP, Popper. Four changes in the last decade: meta-level search, recursion, predicate invention, new technologies (ASP, Prolog, neural nets). The PDF text lost its digits, so no counts are quoted.
limits: Qualitative survey. The authors call their old-vs-new table oversimplified.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for S2/S3: examples, BK, hypothesis space, language bias.

source: Cropper, Dumancic, Evans, Muggleton (2021/22) Inductive logic programming at 30 - search methods
finding: Three search families. Top-down starts general and specialises (can learn recursion, but wasteful). Bottom-up (Golem, relative least-general generalisation) starts from examples and generalises (fast, but long hypotheses, hard for recursion and predicate invention). Progol builds a bottom clause per example and searches between it and the empty clause with A*. Meta-level ILP encodes learning as a solver problem (ASPAL, ILASP, Popper).
numbers: ILASP: select-and-constrain loop driven by uncovered examples. Popper: generate-test-constrain loop that learns constraints from a failed hypothesis.
limits: Authors state there is no standard definition of meta-level ILP.
agent_relevance: Template for an agent loop: generate a rule, test on examples, turn the failure into a constraint on the next generation.

source: Cropper, Dumancic, Evans, Muggleton (2021/22) Inductive logic programming at 30 - recursion and predicate invention
finding: Older systems that rely on bottom-clause construction need examples of both base and inductive cases to learn recursion. Meta-interpretive learning (MIL, Metagol) uses higher-order metarules such as chain P(A,B):-Q(A,C),R(C,B) to learn recursion and invent predicates. Metarules force decomposition into reusable parts.
numbers: Example: a drop-four-elements program uses one invented predicate twice. MetagolDF multi-task learning reuses solved tasks; Forgetgol adds forgetting because too much irrelevant BK hurts.
limits: Metagol is efficient only if the user gives suitable metarules; otherwise 'almost useless' (authors).
agent_relevance: Invented helper concepts shrink the answer and ease search. Let the agent name sub-concepts, but keep their number bounded.

source: Cropper, Dumancic, Evans, Muggleton (2021/22) Inductive logic programming at 30 - limitations
finding: Open problems: tools hard to use, brittle language bias (metarules, mode declarations), few new datasets (most work still on very old ones), choosing relevant BK, noisy and ambiguous raw data, probabilistic ILP, explainability evidence, merging with neural methods.
numbers: Complementarity list: neural nets scale and tolerate noise and raw data but are data hungry and opaque; ILP is data efficient and readable but weak on scale, noise and raw input.
limits: Authors' own view, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: An LLM can supply the perception and noise tolerance ILP lacks; ILP-style checking supplies exact coverage. Hybrid is the natural design.

source: Cropper, Dumancic, Muggleton (2020) Turning 30: New ideas in ILP
finding: Short IJCAI survey that precedes the longer one. Same four themes and same old-vs-new comparison. Notes that recursion lets ILP generalise from small numbers of examples.
numbers: Digits missing in extracted text; no experimental numbers.
limits: Overlaps heavily with the 2021 survey; count as one source.
agent_relevance: Do not count twice as independent evidence.

source: Muggleton (1991) Inductive logic programming (New Generation Computing)
finding: Founding paper that names the field: learn logic programs from examples and BK. Setting as cited by the 2021 survey: find a hypothesis covering as many positives and as few negatives as possible.
numbers: Not opened (paywalled). Only the survey's description is used.
limits: Not read this session; claim comes from the survey text.
agent_relevance: Cite the setting, not new facts, from this paper.

source: Muggleton and De Raedt (1994) Inductive logic programming: theory and methods (J. Logic Programming)
finding: Standard formal reference: ILP framed as search over clauses ordered by generality (theta-subsumption), with inverse resolution and refinement operators.
numbers: Not opened; the fetch returned an HTML page, not the paper.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for a 'more general than' ordering of rule candidates.

source: Muggleton (1995) Inverse entailment and Progol (New Generation Computing)
finding: Progol builds the most specific clause that entails a seed example (bottom clause) and searches clauses below it. Described this way in the 2021 survey.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Survey description only.
agent_relevance: Idea: use one example to bound the rule space from below. A prompt can do the same: write the most specific rule explaining this one case, then generalise.

source: Cropper and Morel (2021) Learning programs by learning from failures (Popper)
finding: Popper runs generate, test, constrain. A failed hypothesis gives constraints: too general prunes its generalisations, too specific prunes its specialisations. It supports recursion, infinite domains, lists, numbers and minimal programs.
numbers: Button-pressing task: Popper learns a 10-literal program in both the small (p=20) and big (p=200) dataset; unconstrained Enumerate manages 3 buttons (small) and 1 button (big). Metagol: largest n is 4 (50 s vs Popper 1 s) small, 3 (57 s vs 8 s) big.
limits: Authors warn comparison is hard: different biases per system; Aleph and ILASP3 handle noise, Metagol and Popper do not.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2/G3: learning from the actual failing case prunes search far better than blind retry.

source: Cropper and Morel (2021) Learning programs by learning from failures (Popper) - grid and list tasks
finding: On a grid world, Metagol is faster at 10x10 (1 s vs 9 s for Popper) but times out above grid size 20. On list transformation (10 runs, 5-minute limit, 50% = failure default), Popper equals or beats Enumerate, Metagol and Aleph, except finddup where Metagol is 2% higher.
numbers: Evens: Enumerate 159 s vs Popper 4 s. Scaling with examples: Popper fine at 20,000 examples; Metagol falls to 50% near 10,000. Example length 50 and 500: Popper under 1 s; Metagol 20 s and 54 s. ILASP failed to ground the Prolog form.
limits: Own benchmarks, synthetic, 10 repeats; 0.1 s test timeout per example.
agent_relevance: Rule checking cost grows only with test cost, so a code-run checker scales well with number of examples.

source: Evans and Grefenstette (2018) Learning explanatory rules from noisy data (dILP)
finding: dILP makes ILP differentiable: clauses get learned weights, forward chaining uses fuzzy truth values, trained by gradient descent. It solved moderately complex tasks with recursion and predicate invention (Fizz-Buzz with several invented predicates; invented transitive closure in 100% of runs on one task).
numbers: 20 symbolic tasks, 200 random initialisations each; success = test MSE below 1e-4. Compared to Metagol. Fizz-Buzz: Grus's MLP trained on 100-1024 failed on every run on the held-out numbers below 100; dILP generalised.
limits: Large memory use, so only nullary, unary and binary predicates; chess strategy and robot-waiter tasks too big. One task solved in only about 30% of initialisations. Authors say a clean comparison with Metagol is hard.
agent_relevance: Rules with variables generalise where memorising nets do not. Argues for forcing an explicit rule rather than direct answers.

source: Evans and Grefenstette (2018) Learning explanatory rules from noisy data (dILP) - noise and ambiguity
finding: dILP degrades smoothly with mislabelled data, unlike symbolic ILP where a single bad label can break learning. With a pre-trained MNIST net feeding it, it learned from images.
numbers: At 10% mislabelled, a perfect answer in 5 of 6 tasks; some good answers at 20-30%. MNIST classifier 98% accurate, so the both-correct ceiling is about 96%; dILP kept low error with 70% of digit pairs never seen; the MLP baseline did not.
limits: Small tasks; six noise tasks.
agent_relevance: Treat one failing example as a signal, not proof the whole rule is wrong, when labels may be noisy.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: GPT-4 first writes many natural-language hypotheses, each is turned into a Python program, and programs are run on the training examples with up to 3 rounds of execution feedback. Programs that pass are applied to the test input. This is the LLM version of ILP's generate and test.
numbers: ARC random 100-problem subset, top-1: direct prompting 17%; program only 23%; LLM-summarised hypotheses (64 -> 8, 8 programs each) 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written LARC hypotheses about the same; Icecuber DSL search 43%. GPT-4 had a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; of those, 33 (67%) led to correct programs.
limits: 100-task subset; GPT-4 only in main run; ARC grids given as text. Summaries became vague and sometimes dropped the right hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for S2/S3: propose several rules in words, then code them and check against examples.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR) - other datasets
finding: Hypotheses help on 1D-ARC and List Functions, but not on SyGuS string tasks, where plain program generation already works.
numbers: SyGuS (89 tasks): GPT-4 94.3% with 8 programs and 2 feedback rounds, the same 94.3% with hypotheses; CrossBeam 74.8%; 3 of the 5 failures had wrong examples. List Functions (100 tasks): 31, 59, 69 across the three settings of Table 5 (column labels read from garbled text: likely direct, program only, full). Chain-of-thought without programs on ARC: 19%.
limits: Table columns read from garbled text; verify before quoting. Code generation, not language alone, gives much of the gain.
agent_relevance: Boundary: an abstract-rule step pays off where examples are few and the rule is hard to see; not where code search already works.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: inductive reasoning with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Propose-select-refine loop with a symbolic interpreter. LMs are good at proposing rules but poor at applying their own rules. Using the LM itself as interpreter (self-refine) removes most of the gain.
numbers: GPT-4 on ACRE, MiniSCAN, List Functions, MiniARC. MiniSCAN task accuracy: 0% with IO, SC and self-refine; up to about 95% with refinement plus symbolic parser. ACRE raw accuracy: IO 64.0, SC 65.0, SR 70.0, best refinement 82.5.
limits: Single main model (GPT-4); Claude-2, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B in appendix show similar direction but lower. Numbers read from a garbled table. Refinement can overfit seen examples on MiniSCAN (T=3,N=1 beat T=3,N=5).
agent_relevance: Strong reason for G2: the checker must be code, not the model. The model that wrote the rule cannot be trusted to execute it.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: inductive reasoning with hypothesis refinement (ICLR) - OOD and human comparison
finding: Rule-based answers lose less accuracy on longer lists than direct IO answers. Majority voting alone does not help; the gain needs selection with feedback. Human MiniSCAN accuracy about 80% (range 65 to 88).
numbers: List Functions task accuracy IID vs OOD: IO 39.6 -> 32.0 vs rule 61.2 -> 62.4 (from figure labels; verify). MiniARC with task-specific heuristics 17.8% raw / 14.6% task, no better than without.
limits: Figure values read from extracted labels; one model.
agent_relevance: Support for holding out longer or larger cases as the G3 test.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Language models as inductive reasoners (DEER)
finding: Moves induction from formal logic to natural language: rules in words from facts in words. Argues ILP needs preprocessed symbolic input, is fragile to label error and cannot treat synonyms as equal. Builds DEER and a five-module pipeline (CoLM) that proposes rules then filters them.
numbers: DEER: 1.2k rule-fact pairs, 6 topics; 95.5% judged correct by 4 graduate students. DEERLET: 846 tuples (546 train, 100 val, 200 test). Base GPT-J (6B) beats the random-fill baseline; the full pipeline beats both. CoLM is worse on history and physics, where rules are abstract and vary.
limits: Dataset written by one expert (first author). Small models (GPT-J 6B; LLaMA in appendix). Automatic metrics proposed by the authors.
agent_relevance: Filters for consistent with facts, not trivial, general are cheap screens on rule candidates; some can be code-checked.

source: Gandarela, Carvalho, Freitas (2025) Inductive learning of logical theories with LLMs: an expressivity-graded analysis (AAAI)
finding: LLMs with feedback from a logic engine were compared against Popper on rule-set induction at several structure levels. Largest LLMs are competitive, especially under noise, but long predicate chains are the main obstacle, more than rule expressivity.
numbers: RuDaS datasets: 5 per category, size XS (50-100 examples), noise/missing/open-world all 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 = 105 datasets, 35 per rate. GPT-3.5/4 average F1 difference about 0.25 vs Popper (as written in the source). LLMs about 3 orders of magnitude faster. No LLM beat Popper on CHAIN at any noise level. Llama3-8B far weaker (Mixtral 11x higher F1 at 0.1 noise).
limits: Synthetic datasets; compute not comparable; LLM theories sometimes had syntax errors and invalid logic.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM to track long chains of relations. Break chains into counted steps and check the theory with a solver.

source: Li et al. (2025) MIRAGE: evaluating and explaining inductive reasoning process in language models (ICLR)
finding: On a synthetic set that tests both rule induction (RI) and example inference (EI), LLMs often answer new cases correctly without the correct rule. They behave as neighbour-based reasoners: they lean on observed facts close in feature space.
numbers: GPT-4o: CoT lowers accuracy by up to 18% and 22% on the two tasks versus few-shot direct answers; with self-refine, EI accuracy exceeds RI accuracy by 16% on average. 200 questions per test. Hypothesis refinement and self-refine do not close the gap.
limits: Synthetic Add/Map style tasks; GPT-4o main; the mechanism claim comes from controlled variation, not model internals.
agent_relevance: Warning for S2/S3: a correct answer does not prove a correct rule. Score the rule on cases far from the examples.

source: Muggleton, Lin, Tamaddoni-Nezhad (2014/15) Meta-interpretive learning
finding: MIL: learn by finding substitutions for higher-order variables in metarules, using a meta-interpreter. Source of Metagol. Described by the 2021 survey.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Survey description only.
agent_relevance: Metarules are program templates; analogue is a rule-shape template in the prompt.

source: Cropper and Muggleton (2016) Metagol system
finding: Metagol does iterative deepening over number of clauses and does not remember failed clauses, which the Popper paper names as its main inefficiency.
numbers: Not opened; the inefficiency claim comes from the Popper paper (opened).
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Remembering failures is the gain; log failed rule shapes in the agent.

source: Law, Russo, Broda (2014-2020) ILASP: learning answer set programs
finding: ILASP learns ASP programs with choice rules and constraints, brave and cautious learning, noise handling. Described by the 2021 survey; example: Hamiltonian-graph definition learned from examples.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Survey description only.
agent_relevance: Rules about what must never hold (constraints) are useful candidates beside positive rules.

source: Rule (2020) The child as hacker (List Functions)
finding: Human concept-learning dataset of list functions with human baselines; used as a benchmark by Wang et al. and Qiu et al.
numbers: Not opened; only referenced as a dataset in two opened papers.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Human baselines exist for List Functions, useful for calibration.

source: Evans and Grefenstette (2018) - related work on neural rule learners
finding: Earlier differentiable rule learners (Yang et al. 2016) learned only individual clauses; dILP learns whole programs with invented predicates and recursion.
numbers: No numbers; related-work paragraph.
limits: Authors' own framing.
agent_relevance: Neural rule learning is an older neighbour of LLM rule proposing.
